title: What is a base class (superclass), and how does it differ from an abstract class?
shortTitle: What is a base class and how it differs from an abstract class

s1_definition.profdef: A base class, also called a superclass or parent class, is any class that another class extends to inherit its fields and methods; it is simply the class higher in an inheritance chain and can itself be instantiated. An abstract class is a special kind of base class declared with the abstract keyword that cannot be instantiated on its own and may declare abstract methods without a body that subclasses must implement; it exists to define a partial, shared template that is only completed by concrete subclasses. So every abstract class is a base class, but a base class need not be abstract.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a base class is like a general Account form that already works and can be filled in and used directly, while also serving as the starting point that specialised forms build on. An abstract class is like a template form stamped Not For Direct Use that deliberately leaves certain boxes blank, such as how interest is calculated, and insists that each specific account type, savings or current, fill in those blank boxes before any real form of that type can exist. You can hand a customer the general account form, but you can never hand them the blank template itself; they must receive a completed, specific version.
s1_definition.oneliner: A base class is any parent class that can be instantiated and extended, while an abstract class is a non-instantiable base class that defines a partial template with abstract methods subclasses must implement.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A base class, also called a superclass or parent class, is any class that another class extends to inherit its fields and methods; it is simply the class higher in an inheritance chain and can itself be instantiated. An abstract class is a special kind of base class declared with the abstract keyword that cannot be instantiated on its own and may declare abstract methods without a body that subclasses must implement; it exists to define a partial, shared template that is only completed by concrete subclasses. So every abstract class is a base class, but a base class need not be abstract.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a base class is like a general Account form that already works and can be filled in and used directly, while also serving as the starting point that specialised forms build on. An abstract class is like a template form stamped Not For Direct Use that deliberately leaves certain boxes blank, such as how interest is calculated, and insists that each specific account type, savings or current, fill in those blank boxes before any real form of that type can exist. You can hand a customer the general account form, but you can never hand them the blank template itself; they must receive a completed, specific version.

**One line to remember:** A base class is any parent class that can be instantiated and extended, while an abstract class is a non-instantiable base class that defines a partial template with abstract methods subclasses must implement.

sections.s2_technical:
A base class, or superclass, is defined purely by position in the hierarchy: if B extends A, then A is the base class of B. There is nothing special in A's declaration; it is an ordinary class that can have fields, constructors, and concrete methods, and it can be instantiated with new. Any concrete class can be a base class simply by being extended.

An abstract class adds constraints and capabilities through the abstract keyword. It cannot be instantiated directly, so you cannot write new on it; you can only instantiate a concrete subclass. It may declare abstract methods, which have a signature but no body, and any concrete subclass must implement all of them or itself be abstract:

```java
abstract class Account {          // abstract base class — no direct new
    protected BigDecimal balance;
    abstract BigDecimal interest(); // no body — subclass must implement
    BigDecimal balance() { return balance; } // concrete shared method
}
class SavingsAccount extends Account {
    BigDecimal interest() { return balance.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.065")); } // required
}
```

So an abstract class mixes shared concrete behavior, which subclasses inherit, with required abstract behavior, which subclasses must supply. A plain base class, by contrast, provides only concrete behavior and leaves nothing mandatory for subclasses, since all its methods already have bodies that a subclass may optionally override.

The differences stated plainly: a base class can be instantiated while an abstract class cannot; a base class has no abstract methods while an abstract class may; a base class is a role any class can play when extended while an abstract class is a deliberate design choice marked with a keyword; and an abstract class is used when some behavior is genuinely undefined at the parent level and must be completed by each subclass, whereas a plain base class is used when the parent is a complete, usable thing that also happens to be extended.

A senior point is to choose an abstract class when you have real shared state and shared method implementations plus a few operations that must differ per subtype, which an interface alone cannot express as cleanly; use a plain base class when the parent is itself a valid, complete entity. Another senior point is that marking a class abstract communicates intent, that it is incomplete by design and must not be used directly, which prevents misuse that a plain base class cannot prevent.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A general Account was used both directly for simple records and as a parent for specialised accounts, which is a plain base class. This is exactly the base-class role.

Problem 2 — Interest calculation genuinely differs by account type and has no sensible default at the parent level, so Account was made abstract with an abstract interest method that each subclass must implement. This is exactly the abstract-class use case.

The code defines an abstract `Account` with shared concrete behavior and an abstract interest method, two concrete subclasses `SavingsAccount` and `CurrentAccount`, and a `BaseVsAbstractDemo` main class that shows subclasses completing the template and the abstract class refusing direct instantiation.

sections.s5_journey:
The inputs are a SavingsAccount for SAV2001 with balance 1000000.00 and a CurrentAccount for CUR3001 with balance 250000.00, both held as Account.

Step 1: The attempt to instantiate the abstract Account directly is left as a comment because it does not compile, demonstrating that an abstract class cannot be created with new.

Step 2: The two concrete subclasses are created. Each one implements monthlyInterest, which is required because Account declares it abstract, so the subclasses are complete and instantiable.

Step 3: Iterating the list, the inherited concrete method balance returns each account's balance directly, showing shared behavior that the abstract base class provided with a body.

Step 4: Calling monthlyInterest uses dynamic dispatch to run each subclass's own implementation, so the savings account computes interest from its rate while the current account returns zero.

Step 5: The projectedBalance method, defined concretely in the abstract base but calling the abstract monthlyInterest, combines shared logic with subtype-specific behavior, producing a projected balance per account, which illustrates how an abstract class blends completed and deferred behavior.

```
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: SAV2001 balance=1000000.00 monthlyInterest=5416.67 projected=1005416.67
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: CUR3001 balance=250000.00 monthlyInterest=0 projected=250000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  abstract Account (cannot be newed)
    │ shared: balance(), projectedBalance()
    │ deferred: monthlyInterest()  (abstract)
    │
    ├─ SavingsAccount.monthlyInterest() = balance × 6.5%/12 → 5416.67
    │     projectedBalance() = balance + interest → 1005416.67
    │
    └─ CurrentAccount.monthlyInterest() = 0 → projected = 250000.00

  Account a = new Account(...)  ← COMPILE ERROR (abstract)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Account Type Hierarchy ═══

  ┌────────┐  REST  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Client │───────→│ Interest Service   │  works with Account abstraction
  └────────┘        └───────┬──────────┘
                            │ monthlyInterest() dispatched per subtype
                            ▼
                 Savings (rate-based) / Current (zero) / future types

```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Base Class vs Abstract Class ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Template Method: projectedBalance() calls abstract      │
  │     monthlyInterest(); subclasses fill the step          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  O: new account type = new subclass, no base edits       │
  │  L: every subclass works wherever Account is expected    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │   <<abstract>> Account        │ cannot be instantiated
  │  # accountId: String          │
  │  # balance: BigDecimal        │
  │  + balance(): BigDecimal      │ concrete (shared)
  │  + projectedBalance()         │ concrete (template)
  │  + monthlyInterest(): BigDec  │ ABSTRACT (deferred)
  └───────────────┬───────────────┘
      extends      │      extends
      ▼                   ▼
  ┌───────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────┐
  │  SavingsAccount    │  │  CurrentAccount    │
  │ + monthlyInterest()│  │ + monthlyInterest()│
  └───────────────────┘  └───────────────────┘

  Differences (in sentences):
    base class  : instantiable, all methods have bodies, parent role
    abstract    : not instantiable, may have abstract methods, template

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. new Account(...) → COMPILE ERROR (abstract)
  2. new SavingsAccount(...) → complete, instantiable
  3. acc.balance() → inherited concrete
  4. acc.monthlyInterest() → subclass override (dynamic dispatch)
  5. acc.projectedBalance() → shared logic + deferred step
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A base class, which people also call a superclass or parent class, is simply any class that another class extends to inherit its fields and methods. It is defined by position in the hierarchy, not by any special keyword, and it is an ordinary class that can have constructors and concrete methods and can be instantiated directly with new. Any concrete class becomes a base class the moment another class extends it.

An abstract class is a special kind of base class declared with the abstract keyword. It cannot be instantiated on its own, so I can never write new on it; I can only instantiate a concrete subclass. It may declare abstract methods, which have a signature but no body, and every concrete subclass must implement all of them or itself be declared abstract. So an abstract class is a partial, shared template that is only completed by its subclasses.

The differences follow from that. A base class can be instantiated while an abstract class cannot. A plain base class has only concrete methods with bodies, which subclasses may optionally override, while an abstract class can mix shared concrete behavior that subclasses inherit with required abstract behavior that subclasses must supply. And a base class is a role any class can play when extended, whereas making a class abstract is a deliberate design statement that it is incomplete and must not be used directly. The relationship is that every abstract class is a base class, but not every base class is abstract.

The way I decide in banking code is this: I use an abstract class when there is genuine shared state and shared method implementations plus a few operations that must differ per subtype, like an Account that shares balance handling but defers interest calculation to each account type. I showed a savings account computing rate-based interest and a current account returning zero, both through the same abstract parent, with a concrete projectedBalance method that calls the deferred interest step, which is the Template Method pattern. I use a plain base class instead when the parent is itself a complete, usable entity that also happens to be extended. So my complete answer is that a base class is any instantiable parent, an abstract class is a non-instantiable base class that defines a template with abstract methods subclasses must implement, and I choose abstract when the parent is deliberately incomplete.
